statement: In people who died in Finland in 1995–2000 of a poisoning that a forensic pathologist certified as due to alcohol, a single drug or both, deaths in which the benzodiazepine temazepam was found together with alcohol (at least 0.50 parts per thousand), compared with deaths from alcohol alone, were associated with a lower blood alcohol concentration measured after death: median 2.5 against 3.3 parts per thousand by weight (57 against 615 deaths), a difference the paper puts at 0.8 (24%; Mann–Whitney P < 0.001) by a method it does not name, with a 95% interval of about −1.0 to −0.6 that it shows only in a figure (editors' reading; Koski et al., 2003). Within the temazepam group, the half with the higher temazepam concentration had died at the lower blood alcohol (median 2.1 against 2.9; printed difference 0.9, P < 0.001), and setting aside the 18 deaths in which temazepam was below its therapeutic range (under 0.4 mg/L) left a median of 2.2 (95% CI 2.1 to 2.5) in the other 39. The authors read these lower levels as a combined toxic effect of temazepam and alcohol, growing with the temazepam concentration; the design cannot show that, or any risk. Only people who died were counted, so nobody who took both and lived is in the data, and nothing was adjusted although the groups were unlike: the alcohol-only deaths were older (mean age 53 against 48) and more often men (88 against 67 in 100), and all but one were recorded as accidents, none as a suicide, while 11 of the 57 temazepam deaths were recorded as suicides and 36 as accidents. Which group a death joined depended on the cause the pathologist certified (alcohol poisoning for 33 of the 57 temazepam deaths, alone or as the more important cause, and drug poisoning for 24); low concentrations of other benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide or their breakdown products) were allowed in the drug groups and were found in 30 in 100 of the temazepam deaths but in none of the alcohol-only deaths, which had to be free of every other substance; temazepam was above the therapeutic range the paper quotes in 26 of the 57; and every concentration was measured after death. Of the nine drugs studied this way, temazepam's difference was the fourth smallest (citalopram 0.3, not significant; zopiclone and diltiazem 0.6; levomepromazine 0.9; amitriptyline, propoxyphene, doxepin and promazine 1.5 to 1.9), and temazepam and zopiclone had the lowest fatal toxicity index (deaths per amount sold, 0.9 each); the authors say this ordering reflects how the drugs are used, some taken deliberately in overdose, as well as their own toxicity. Temazepam was the only benzodiazepine among the nine (drugs found in at least 20 such poisonings); the authors' 2002 paper on other benzodiazepines, which they cite as finding no lower blood alcohol with diazepam, chlordiazepoxide or desmethyldiazepam at concentrations up to 1 mg/L, was not read, and alprazolam (Xanax) was not studied. What alcohol and benzodiazepines do to breathing together is described only second-hand: a 2002 narrative review by one author (Tanaka, 2002) states that high doses of the two depress breathing synergistically (more than the sum of each), citing three single-dose studies that its own table describes only by pharmacokinetic measures, and gives no breathing measurement, number or dose for it; the Finnish authors call the combined effect of alcohol and drugs that depress the nervous system generally considered additive and usually not a matter of blood levels (a general statement, not their finding). In the review's table of eight single-dose study arms, alcohol did not change the benzodiazepine's pharmacokinetics in five, alprazolam's among them, and changed them in three, in both directions, although its abstract says that metabolism is in general delayed. The review also lists 39 published deaths in which both alcohol and a benzodiazepine were found (from 10 reports of 1988 to 1999, 25 of them from one Canadian series of triazolam deaths; 3 with alprazolam, each with other drugs), with no count of people who took both and lived. No study read here measured breathing, sedation or how often harm follows in living people who combine alcohol with a benzodiazepine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Is it dangerous to mix Xanax and alcohol? The studies read here did not measure the risk, and Xanax itself was barely studied. In Finnish death records from 1995 to 2000, people who died with alcohol and the benzo temazepam had less alcohol in their blood than people who died of alcohol alone: in the middle of each group, 2.5 against 3.3 parts per thousand, about a quarter lower. Among the temazepam deaths, those with more temazepam had died at lower alcohol levels still. The authors read this as temazepam and alcohol being more toxic together. But only deaths were counted, not people who took both and lived, and the two groups were different people: the alcohol-only deaths were older and more often men, and none was recorded as a suicide, while 11 of the 57 temazepam deaths were. A 2002 review says that high doses of alcohol and benzos together slow breathing more than the two would add up to, but it shows no breathing measurement for this. In five of the eight single-dose tests it lists, alcohol did not change benzo blood levels, Xanax's included. It also lists 39 published deaths with both alcohol and a benzo in the blood; 3 involved Xanax, all with other drugs as well.
population: People who died in Finland in 1995–2000 whose deaths were investigated toxicologically at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, with the cause certified by a forensic pathologist as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (1006 deaths; 615 from alcohol alone, mean age 53, 88% men; 57 from alcohol with temazepam, mean age 48, 67% men); for the review's material, published single-dose studies of alcohol with a benzodiazepine and 39 published deaths with both in the blood, selected by one author
exposure: Temazepam found in femoral blood after death (counted from 0.1 mg/L, below the bottom of its quoted therapeutic range, 0.4 mg/L) together with alcohol at 0.50 parts per thousand or more, the death certified as poisoning by alcohol, temazepam or both; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam allowed; amounts taken, timing and route unknown. In the review, alcohol given with single benzodiazepine doses in studies (conditions as printed), and both found in published deaths
comparator: Deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol alone, with no other substance found in the screens (615); within the temazepam group, the half with the lower against the half with the higher temazepam concentration; no living people and no adjustment
outcome: Median blood alcohol concentration after death (parts per thousand, mass per mass, femoral blood), compared by Mann–Whitney tests; in the review, a statement on breathing with no measurement reported, and pharmacokinetic measures from single-dose studies

The Results text gives 0.6–0.7 for the zopiclone, levomepromazine and temazepam groups, which matches neither Table 3 (0.6, 0.9, 0.8) nor the differences of the printed medians (0.6, 0.7, 0.8). Temazepam split at 0.7 mg/L (Table 4, p. 285): 28 deaths at or below, median 2.9; 29 above, 2.1; printed difference 0.9 (the medians differ by 0.8), P < 0.001. Without the 18 deaths with temazepam under 0.4 mg/L: median 2.2 (95% CI 2.1–2.5) in 39 (Results, p. 283). Temazepam concentrations (Table 2, p. 283): median 0.8 mg/L against a quoted therapeutic range of 0.4–0.9; below the range 18, within it 13, above it 26 (46%); other benzodiazepines at low concentration in 30% of the temazepam group. Groups (Table 1, p. 283): alcohol only, 544 of 615 men (88%), mean age 53 (23–85), 614 accidental (99.8%), no suicide; temazepam, 38 of 57 men (67%), mean age 48 (32–72), 36 accidental (63%), 11 suicides (19%); listed as alcohol poisoning 33 (printed as 46%; 33 of 57 is 58%, editors' calculation) and as drug poisoning 24 (42%). Other drugs, printed differences: citalopram 0.3 (P > 0.05), diltiazem 0.6 (P = 0.006), zopiclone 0.6, levomepromazine 0.9, amitriptyline 1.5, propoxyphene 1.6, doxepin 1.6, promazine 1.9 (each P < 0.001). No breathing figure anywhere in the review. Table 4 (p. 72): 39 deaths (editors' count; no total printed) from 10 reports (references 49–58), 25 from Joynt (1993); 32 rows name triazolam; blood ethanol 0.1–3.2 mg/mL (editors' median 1.7); triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL, the top of the range the table quotes from one case report, in 13 of the 32 (editors' count, one trace included); alprazolam in 3 rows (200 ng/mL with triazolam and others; a trace with triazolam, diazepam and nordiazepam; 210 ng/mL with others).

evidence.extracted: 1006 Finnish autopsy cases toxicologically investigated at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, in 1995–2000, whose cause of death a forensic pathologist had established as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (where both, the more important cause cited first on the death certificate). Femoral blood taken at autopsy into 1% sodium fluoride and kept at 4 °C; alcohol measured in every sample and a broad drug screen in about 83% of cases, at the pathologist's request; blood alcohol given in parts per thousand, mass per mass. The nine drugs were those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type; limit of quantitation 0.02 mg/L for temazepam. Each drug's lowest included concentration was the bottom of its therapeutic range, except temazepam, counted from 0.1 mg/L because effects can occur below the therapeutic level; mixed poisonings needed blood alcohol of at least 0.50. The 615 deaths from alcohol alone were free of every other substance in the screens; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam were allowed in the mixed groups.

risk_of_bias.note: Very serious (card sc_koski_2003: ROBINS-E very high). The comparison is unadjusted, between two groups of people who died that differ in what most plausibly sets the alcohol level at death: age (mean 53 against 48), sex (88 against 67 in 100 men), manner of death (no suicide among the 615 alcohol-only deaths, 11 of the 57 with temazepam) and, unmeasured, tolerance and drinking pattern. Group membership rests on the certified cause; low concentrations of other benzodiazepines were allowed in the drug groups only (30 in 100 of the temazepam deaths), and the authors' statement that they did not change the medians comes without numbers; temazepam was counted from 0.1 mg/L where the other drugs started at their therapeutic range; every concentration was measured after death; 19 tests were run without correction. The difference is statistically clear (P < 0.001; the plotted interval does not include zero), but these differences between the groups could produce it without any effect of temazepam.

inconsistency.note: One study carries the comparison, so consistency across studies cannot be judged; inside it, the concentration split and the analysis without the below-range deaths point the same way.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one benzodiazepine (temazepam), deaths certified as poisoning in Finland, and blood alcohol at death as the outcome, which the statement names. The statement does not extend the finding to alprazolam (Xanax) or to other benzodiazepines, and it says that the risk for living people, which is what people ask, was not measured.

imprecision.note: 57 against 615 deaths; the interval read from Figure 1, about −1.0 to −0.6, excludes zero. An interval is printed as text only for the analysis without the below-range deaths (2.1 to 2.5).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: a retrospective records analysis with no protocol; the authors' companion paper on other benzodiazepines was not read.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the split by temazepam concentration is unadjusted, and deliberate overdoses may sit in the higher half (26 of the 57 above the quoted therapeutic range).

grade.reasoning: Observational records of deaths certified as poisoning: starts low; risk of bias −2 gives very low (the floor). The claim is worded as an association among people who died; the authors' reading of it as a combined toxic effect is reported, not adopted, and no risk is stated, because none can be computed without the people who took both and lived. The breathing sentences rest on one narrative review that shows no data for them (said to be second-hand in the statement) and on a general statement in the Finnish paper; they qualify the claim and are not rated. The review's pharmacokinetic table and its list of 39 published deaths are its author's selections, with no stated search and no appraisal (card sc_tanaka_2002), and are described as such; the published deaths have no comparison group and are not counted as replication. Status single study: one records study carries the comparison; the authors' 2002 paper on other benzodiazepines and the 1980s post-mortem studies of other drugs with alcohol that they cite were not read. Risk facts only: amounts appear as study conditions and measurements after death, never as guidance.

The name Xanax for alprazolam comes from the site's identity record (data/identity/benzodiazepines.json), not from these papers.
